lessons.title: Working in a tractor workshop
lessons.html:
The workshop and your place in it

A tractor workshop may be on a farm, at a dealership or at a co-op in town. It is a busy place with heavy machines, sharp tools, oil, fuel and electricity. Everyone must work safely and as a team. As a new mechanic or assistant, you need to know how the workplace runs.

Who does what

  • Workshop foreman or manager: plans the work, gives out job cards and checks quality.
  • Qualified mechanic: diagnoses faults and does the main repairs.
  • Service mechanic: does routine services and simple repairs.
  • Mechanic assistant: helps the mechanic, cleans parts, fetches tools and keeps the bay tidy.
  • Parts person: issues and orders parts.
  • Customer or farm manager: owns the tractor and needs it back working.

The job card

Every job starts with a job card. It shows the tractor, the customer, the hour meter reading, the problem and the work to be done. You write down the work you did, parts used and the time spent. Never start work without a job card, and never throw it away.

Good work habits

  1. Arrive on time and ready to work.
  2. Listen to instructions and ask if you do not understand.
  3. Keep your bay, tools and floor clean.
  4. Look after the customer's tractor. Use seat and fender covers.
  5. Tell the foreman about problems early. Do not hide mistakes.
  6. Do not use your phone while working on a machine.

Rights and duties

Under the OHS Act 85 of 1993, your employer must give you a safe workplace, training and protective equipment. You must follow safety rules, use your PPE and report unsafe conditions and injuries. You have the right to refuse work that is clearly dangerous and to report it.

lessons.title: Safety, communication and the environment
lessons.html:
Basic workshop safety

Most workshop injuries come from a few causes: slips and trips, lifting, crushing under machines, cuts, burns and eye injuries. Simple rules prevent most of them.

  • Wear overalls, safety boots and safety glasses. Add gloves, ear plugs or a face shield when the job needs them.
  • Clean up oil and diesel spills at once.
  • Never work under a tractor held up only by a jack. Use proper stands or blocks.
  • Take the key out and apply the handbrake before working on a tractor.
  • Lift with your legs, keep your back straight and ask for help with heavy parts.
  • Know where the fire extinguishers and first aid box are.

Talking and listening

Good communication prevents accidents and mistakes. Speak clearly. Repeat instructions back to check you understood: So you want me to drain the engine oil and change the filter on the John Deere in bay 2? Use the right names for parts. If a customer asks you about their tractor, be polite and refer technical questions to the mechanic or foreman.

Reading information

You will read job cards, parts lists, service manuals, labels and safety signs. Learn the common safety signs: red circle means do not, blue circle means you must, yellow triangle means warning, green means safe condition or first aid.

Looking after the environment

Used oil, filters, coolant, batteries and old tyres can harm soil and water. On a farm, oil spilled near a borehole can poison drinking water.

  1. Drain oil into a drip tray and pour it into the used oil drum.
  2. Put used filters in the marked bin to drain.
  3. Store old batteries upright in the marked area for recycling.
  4. Use absorbent material on spills, never wash oil into the drain or veld.
  5. Keep waste for collection by a registered recycler.

Key points

  • Every job needs a job card that you complete.
  • Wear PPE and never work under a machine held only by a jack.
  • Repeat instructions back to check you understood.
  • Report unsafe conditions, injuries and mistakes.
  • Collect used oil, filters and batteries for recycling.
